list.listitem: Diagnostic evaluation of male infertility includes careful history, physical examination, semen analysis, and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), and testosterone levels if earlier findings are abnormal.C
Semen analysis is the primary assessment tool for male fertility potential.C
Gonadotrophic drugs may be effective for men with idiopathic male factor subfertility.B
There is no evidence to support corticosteroids for antisperm antibodies, varicocele repair, or antibiotics for leukocytes in semen.B
The pregnancy rate for male infertility is 25% in couples not undergoing therapeutic donor insemination.B

background.definition: Infertility in a couple is defined as the inability to achieve conception despite 1 year of regular, unprotected intercourse. Male infertility is defined as any condition in which the male adversely affects the chances of achieving a successful pregnancy with his female partner.

list.listitem: Infertility affects 15% to 20% of couples trying to conceive.
Male infertility alone accounts for nearly 30% of cases; both male and female infertility accounts for an additional 20% of cases.
Therefore, male infertility is at least partly responsible for half of all cases of infertility.

While the prevalence of infertility in developing countries is difficult to assess given inconsistencies in defining infertility, between 8% and 12% of couples around the world have difficulty conceiving a child at some point in their lives, thus affecting 50 to 80 million people.

In the United States, infertility costs are often not covered by health insurance. Therefore, actual expenditures based upon claims data are underestimating both actual expenditures and the financial burden placed on patients.

In 2000, total expenditures for treating primary male infertility were approximately US$17 million. However, adding the cost for assisted reproduction technology cycles placed the total cost at about US $18 billion.
Seminiferous tubule dysfunction (60%-80%) including micro deletions of the Y chromosome.
Testicular disease: primary hypogonadism (10%-15%).
Post-testicular defects: disorders of sperm transport (10%-20%).
Hypothalamic pituitary disorders: secondary hypogonadism (1%-2%).
In a majority of cases, the etiology of male factor infertility is unknown.26
Pathophysiology is often not well understood.
Endocrine abnormalities are common in infertile males.
Obesity is associated with decreased testosterone levels; in massively obese individuals, reduced spermatogenesis and erectile dysfunction result in reduced fertility.
Boxer shorts do not affect fertility.B
Inform men who have a body mass index (BMI) greater than 29 that they are likely to have diminished fertility.C
Inform men that excessive alcohol intake is harmful to semen quality.B

See couples together for the infertility evaluation. Obtain developmental history, chronic medical illnesses, surgical procedures to genitalia, and careful history of environmental, drug, and medication exposures; sexual history; and infections (such as mumps or sexually transmitted disease).C
Diagnostic evaluation of male infertility begins with properly collected semen analysis, with a second analysis if the first is abnormal.C
If semen is abnormal, order FSH, LH, and testosterone tests.C

Meta-analytic study demonstrates that there may be an association between genetics and male infertility- particularly polymorphism of the androgen receptor gene CAG. Increased androgen receptor CAG length is capable of causing male infertility susceptibility and is associated with azoospermia.C

Differential.Differential_Features: "Bag of worms" on palpation of testis

Differential.Differential_Name: Klinefelter's syndrome and other congenital disorders
Differential.Differential_Features: Physical features: small penis, testes not palpable or small, gynecomastia, learning disability
Ejaculation of blood, hematuria, severe pain, visible swelling of testicle
Premature ejaculation, painful ejaculation, retrograde ejaculation, anejaculation
Erectile dysfunction, decreased libido, liver cirrhosis, insulin resistance, high ferritin

list.listitem: Inform people who are worried about their fertility that female fertility deteriorate with age but that the effect of age on male fertility is less clear. See couples who experience difficulty in conceiving together, because both partners are affected by decisions surrounding investigation and treatment.

Take a history of sexual development, any relevant infections (eg, mumps orchitis, sexually transmitted diseases, prostatitis), and drug and environmental exposures (eg, alcohol, radiation therapy, anabolic steroids, and cytotoxic chemotherapy). Obtain a sexual history including libido, intercourse frequency, and previous fertility history.
Premature ejaculation is the most prevalent male sexual dysfunction. Depression is statistically significantly associated with an increased risk of premature ejaculation.

On physical examination, look for evidence of androgen deficiency (eg, loss of secondary male characteristics: skin, genitalia, and breasts). Examine genitals: penis, including the location of the urethral meatus, palpation and size of testes, presence and consistency of both the vasa and epididymides, presence of varicocele, digital rectal examination.
The diagnosis of congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBAVD) is established by physical examination.

Evaluation begins with semen analysis. Semen collection standard instructions: (1) abstinence of 2 to 3 days, (2) collection by masturbation or by intercourse using special condom (does not contain substances reducing quality/quantity of sperm), (3) collection may be at home or laboratory, (4) specimen must be maintained at room or body temperature during transportation and examined within 1 hour of collection and (5) if multiple samples needed, greater than or equal to 7 days between ejaculate.

Normal semen characteristics: volume 1.0 to 6.5 mL/ejaculation; liquefaction time is less than 60 seconds; count 20 to 150 million sperm/mL; 70% or greater normal shape and structure; 60% or greater normal motility; pH 7.1 to 8.0; no WBC or bacteria; 300 mg or greater fructose/100 mL. See for the nomenclature of abnormalities. Other characteristics of normal semen: less than 20% spermatozoa with adherent particles; 52 micromol or greater citric acid/ejaculate; 2.4 micromol or greater zinc/ejaculate; 200 U or greater acid phosphatase/ejaculate.

Order the following initial studies in a man with abnormal semen (confirmed by second semen analysis): FSH, LH, and serum testosterone. If testosterone is low, a repeat total and free testosterone measurement, LH, and FSH should be obtained ().

Perform a postejaculatory urinalysis to diagnose possible retrograde ejaculation in patients with ejaculate volumes of less than 1 mL except with bilateral vasal agenesis or clinical signs of hypogonadism.
Order transrectal ultrasonography in azoospermic patients with palpable vasa and low ejaculate volumes to determine whether ejaculatory duct obstruction exists.

When physical examination of the scrotum is difficult or inadequate (palpable pathology, eg, varicoceles, spermatoceles, absence of vasa), or a testicular mass is suspected, order a scrotal ultrasonography.

Specialized tests on semen (eg, WBC in semen, antisperm antibody, viability test) are not required for diagnosis of male infertility. They may be useful in a small number of patients for identifying a male factor contributing to unexplained infertility, or for selecting therapy such as assisted reproductive technology. Screening for antisperm antibodies should not be offered because there is no evidence of effective treatment to improve fertility.
Offer genetic testing for cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator gene mutations in the female partner before proceeding with treatments that utilize the sperm of men with CBAVD.

Inform men with nonobstructive azoospermia and severe oligospermia (<5 million sperm/mL) of the potential genetic abnormalities associated with azoospermia or severe oligospermia. Offer karyotyping and Y-chromosome analysis to the male who has nonobstructive azoospermia or severe oligospermia prior to performing ICSI. Offer genetic counseling whenever a genetic abnormality is suspected in either the male or female partner and provide it whenever a genetic abnormality is detected.
If the result of the first semen analysis is abnormal, offer a repeat confirmatory test.
See for a suggested diagnostic algorithm.
Consider gonadotrophin drugs for men with idiopathic male factor subfertility, as preliminary data suggest improvement in live birth and pregnancy rates.B
Varicocele repair demonstrates no conclusive evidence in restoring fertility.B
Offer clomiphene plus vitamin E to men with idiopathic male infertility with oligoasthenospermia.B

Gonadotrophins, androgens, bromocriptine, and kinin-enhancing drugs are not effective for men with idiopathic semen abnormalities. Similarly, there is no evidence to support corticosteroids for antisperm antibodies or antibiotics for leukocytes in semen.B

There is insufficient evidence for the comparative efficacy and safety of intrauterine insemination (IUI), in vitro fertilization (IVF), and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) for male infertility.B

Do not offer antibiotic treatment to men with leukocytes in their semen unless there is an identified infection, because there is no evidence that this improves pregnancy rates. Similarly, the value of corticosteroids for men with antisperm antibodies is unknown.

Consider gonadotrophin drugs for men with idiopathic male factor subfertility, which refers to men whose subfertility is not attributable to identifiable causes. A Cochrane review of 6 RCTs involving 456 patients concluded that preliminary findings suggest higher live births and pregnancy rates. Given the methodological shortcomings of the studies, larger trials are needed before gonadotrophins are routinely recommended for men with idiopathic male factor subfertility.

Offer clomiphene plus vitamin E to men with idiopathic male infertility with oligoasthenospermia. In a single RCT (n = 60), couples in whom the male partner was treated with clomiphene 25 mg plus vitamin E 400 IU daily were more likely to achieve pregnancy than control couples (NNT = 4; 95% CI, 2-78).
Do not offer gonadotrophins, androgens, bromocriptine, or kinin-enhancing drugs to men with idiopathic semen abnormalities, because of ineffectiveness.

Oral antioxidants (vitamins C and E, zinc, selenium, folate, carnitine and carotenoids) may positively affect sperm quality and/or motility and improve pregnancy rates in couples with infertile men. There is low-certainty evidence that antioxidant supplementation in subfertile males may improve live birth rates for couples attending fertility clinics. However, a large (n = 2370) randomized, placebo-controlled trial at 4 U.S. centers found no differences in semen quality or live birth rates when the male partner took a daily supplement containing folic acid 5 mg and zinc 30 mg for 6 months.

Although male infertility with a primary endocrine etiology is encountered infrequently in clinical practice, endocrinopathies represent an important category of illnesses amenable to available medical treatments.
Serum 17OH-progesterone is a surrogate biomarker of intratesticular testosterone and may be useful in research and in men receiving gonadotropin therapy for infertility.
Prolonged treatment with recombinant human FSH at high doses led to an evident improvement of sperm count in normogonadotropic infertile patients with idiopathic oligoasthenozoospermia.
Alpha blockers and mast-cell blockers need further evaluation before they can be considered in the treatment of men with semen abnormalities.
Varicocele repair is ineffective in restoring fertility.

Consider surgical sperm recovery before intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) using several different techniques depending on the pathology and wishes of the patient. In all cases, facilities for cryopreservation of spermatozoa should be available.
There is insufficient evidence to recommend any specific sperm retrieval technique (from either the epididymis or the testis) for azoospermic men undergoing ICSI.

Where appropriate expertise is available, men with obstructive azoospermia should be offered surgical correction of epididymal blockage because it is likely to restore patency of the duct and improve fertility. Surgical correction should be considered as an alternative to surgical sperm recovery and IVF.
Evidence for intrauterine insemination (IUI) over timed intercourse is lacking.

Azoospermia, the absence of sperm in ejaculated semen, is the most severe factor in male infertility and is present in approximately 5% of all infertile couples. ICSI has transformed this condition since sperms can be retrieved from either the epididymis or the testis depending upon the type of azoospermia.
Inform couples that ICSI improves fertilization rates compared with in vitro fertilization alone, but once fertilization is achieved, the pregnancy rate is no better than with in vitro fertilization.
The recognized indications for treatment by ICSI include: severe deficits in semen quality, obstructive azoospermia, and nonobstructive azoospermia.
Determine the male karyotype when the indication for ICSI is a severe deficit of semen quality or nonobstructive azoospermia.

The use of donor insemination is considered effective in managing fertility problems associated with the following conditions: obstructive azoospermia, nonobstructive azoospermia, infectious disease in the male partner (eg, HIV), severe rhesus isoimmunization, or severe deficits in semen quality in couples who do not wish to undergo ICSI.
Offer IUI to couples using donor sperm in preference to intracervical insemination because it improves pregnancy rates.
Boxer shorts do not make it more likely to have normal sperm parameters.

Density gradient centrifugation selection of sperm (for assisted reproductive techniques) may affect DNA integrity in approximately 50% of subjects, who then show a much lower probability of pregnancy.
There is considerable uncertainty regarding the effectiveness and safety of psychological and educational interventions and providing preconception advice to improve fertility.
Consider consultation or referral to a fertility specialist when no identifiable and reversible causes of infertility are evident and/or invasive diagnostic testing is required.
In a study of 304 infertile couples with suspected male factor infertility, 73 had therapeutic donor insemination with a 48% pregnancy rate.B
In the same study, the pregnancy rate was 25% for the remaining 231 couples.B
The best predictors of successful pregnancy were shorter duration of infertility and a history of pregnancy in the female partner.B

feature.caption: Nomenclature of Semen Variables.
feature.feature_body:
Diagnosis Definition
Normozoospermia Normal ejaculate
Oligozoospermia Sperm concentration <20 million per mL per ejaculate
Asthenozoospermia <50% spermatozoa with forward progression (categories A and B) or <25% spermatozoa with category A movementa
Teratozoospermia <30% spermatozoa with normal morphology
Azoospermia No spermatozoa in the ejaculate
Aspermia No ejaculate
a Motility categories: (A) rapid progressive motility (covering a distance of at least 20 micrometers per second); (B) slow or sluggish progressive motility; (C) nonprogressive motility; (D) Immotility. Adapted from World Health Organization. WHO Laboratory Manual for the Examination of Human Semen and Sperm-Cervical Mucus Interaction. 3rd. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. 1992.
